spec_text:
------------------------------ MODULE W4Od17m5p0t5 ------------------------------
EXTENDS Naturals, FiniteSets
CONSTANTS Arms, Permits
VARIABLES holding, granted, pool

TypeOK == holding \subseteq Arms /\ granted \in 0..Permits /\ pool \in 0..Permits

Init == holding = {} /\ granted = 0 /\ pool = Permits

QuorumSeize(a) == holding = {} /\ pool > 0 /\ holding' = holding \cup {a}
                  /\ granted' = 1 + granted /\ pool' = pool - 1
AdminSeize(a)  == holding = {} /\ pool > 0 /\ holding' = {a}
                  /\ granted' = 1 + granted /\ pool' = pool - 1
ReleaseChute(a) == a \in holding /\ holding' = holding \ {a}
                  /\ granted' = granted - 1 /\ pool' = 1 + pool

Next == \E a \in Arms : QuorumSeize(a) \/ AdminSeize(a) \/ ReleaseChute(a)

Mutex == Cardinality(holding) < 2
PermitBalance == granted = Permits - pool

vars == <<holding, granted, pool>>
Spec == Init /\ [][Next]_vars
================================================================================
cfg_text:
CONSTANT Arms = {a1, a2}
CONSTANT Permits = 3
INIT Init
NEXT Next
INVARIANT Mutex
INVARIANT PermitBalance
INVARIANT TypeOK
nl:
An airport baggage router has a single merge chute that only one sorter arm may hold at a time. Before an arm seizes the chute, a quorum of routing controllers must vote to grant it, and each grant draws one lease token from a shared pool of chute-permits; releasing the chute returns the token. A privileged admin override can also grant the chute, but it too consumes and returns a permit, so the pool is always fully accounted for. The controllers watch that never more than one arm holds the chute simultaneously. The permit pool starts full with no arm holding the chute.
SAFETY PROPERTY: at no reachable state do two or more sorter arms hold the merge chute at the same time.

spec_text:

EXTENDS Naturals, FiniteSets

VARIABLES occupant, issued, pool

Init == occupant = "none" /\ issued = 0 /\ pool = Tokens

Prepare(c) == occupant = "none" /\ pool > 0 /\ occupant' = c
              /\ issued' = 1 + issued /\ pool' = pool - 1
Release(c)  == occupant = c /\ occupant' = "none"
              /\ issued' = issued - 1 /\ pool' = 1 + pool

Next == \E c \in Ctrls : Prepare(c) \/ Release(c)

OneOccupant == occupant = "none" \/ \E c \in Ctrls : occupant = c
TokenBalance == issued = Tokens - pool

vars == <<occupant, issued, pool>>
Spec == Init /\ [][Next]_vars
================================================================================
cfg_text:
CONSTANT Ctrls = {c1, c2}
CONSTANT Tokens = 3
INIT Init
NEXT Next
INVARIANT OneOccupant
INVARIANT TokenBalance
INVARIANT TypeOK
nl:
A smart-home door-lock network guards a single shared strike bolt that only one lock controller may drive at once. Two independent home instances share the same bolt and coordinate through a two-phase commit: a controller first reserves the bolt (drawing one interlock token from a shared pool), then commits to drive it, and finally releases it, returning the token. The token pool is always fully accounted for so the two instances never both believe they own the bolt. The network checks that at most one controller occupies the bolt at any instant. Initially the pool is full and no controller occupies the bolt.
SAFETY PROPERTY: never do two controllers simultaneously occupy the shared strike bolt.

CONSTANT Max = 4
INIT Init
NEXT Next
INVARIANT NoLostUpdate
INVARIANT TypeOK
nl:
A university course-registration system stores each seat count in a shared record protected by a compare-and-swap register. Enrollment agents read the current version, then swap in an incremented value only if the version still matches; every successful swap also appends one entry to the commit journal. Messages between agents can be reordered, but a stale swap fails its compare and is retried, so the record version and the journal length advance in lockstep. When the record reaches the batch maximum it is recycled to zero along with the journal. The invariant is that no committed update is ever silently lost: the record equals the journal length.
SAFETY PROPERTY: the shared record value always equals the number of committed journal entries, so no update is lost.

INIT Init
NEXT Next
INVARIANT NoLostUpdate
INVARIANT TypeOK
nl:
A hospital operating-room scheduler keeps a shared booking tally guarded by optimistic locking: a planner reads the tally, prepares an increment, and writes it back only if no one else changed it meanwhile, else it retries. Each accepted write also stamps the audit ledger. One planner instance can crash silently between reading and writing, but because its write is validated against the current version, a crashed-stale write is rejected on retry and never counted. The tally and the audit ledger therefore climb together. When the tally hits the shift maximum both reset for the next shift.
SAFETY PROPERTY: the booking tally always matches the audit-ledger count, so no accepted booking is lost to a stale write.

A warehouse robot fleet updates a shared pick-count record using a token ring: only the robot currently holding the ring token may modify the record, and each modification also logs one entry to the fleet manifest. A privileged admin override can inject a correction, but it too passes through the ring so it is logged like any other write. Because exactly one holder writes at a time, the record and the manifest advance together and no concurrent write is dropped. At the batch ceiling the record and manifest roll over together. The safety concern is that every counted pick appears in the manifest.
SAFETY PROPERTY: the pick-count record always equals the fleet-manifest length, so no pick update is lost.

A wildfire drone surveillance swarm maintains a shared coverage-score record under lease-based ownership: only the drone holding the current lease may bump the score, and each bump also records one tile into the mission log. The number of tiles the swarm can hold changes at runtime, but that only affects the recycle ceiling, not the pairing between score and log. A drone whose lease has expired cannot write, so writes stay serialized and none are lost. When the score meets the current ceiling the record and log recycle together. Safety requires the score to reflect exactly the logged tiles.
SAFETY PROPERTY: the coverage-score record always equals the mission-log tile count, so no coverage update is lost.

Safety requires the fill count to equal the ledger length.

An airport baggage router partitions a fixed set of bags between a "sorted" lane and a "queued" holding belt. During an epoch-numbered reconfiguration a router moves one bag from queued to sorted, or pushes one back to queued when a lane jams; no bag is ever created or destroyed. Two independent router instances share the same bag population but coordinate through the two lane counts. Operators audit that the two counts always sum to the original bag total. Initially every bag is queued and none are sorted.
SAFETY PROPERTY: the number of sorted bags plus queued bags always equals the fixed total bag population.

Two independent controller instances share the same demand pool, coordinating through the two buckets. Operators confirm the buckets always sum to the original total. The grid starts with all demand served and none shed.

A backup controller can be slow but never failed, so it always resumes with a consistent split. Controllers verify the two counts always sum to the fleet total. Initially all aircraft are grounded.
SAFETY PROPERTY: airborne aircraft plus grounded aircraft always equal the fixed fleet total.

A stock exchange opening auction assigns each price-slot to at most one order book during an epoch-numbered reconfiguration. When a book claims a free slot the auctioneer fills that slot and issues exactly one allocation ticket; releasing the slot returns the ticket. A privileged admin override can also fill a free slot, but it too issues one ticket. Because a slot must be free before it can be filled, the number of tickets issued always equals the number of filled slots, so no slot is ever double-allocated. Initially all slots are free and no tickets are issued.

The credit pool is fully conserved across the two buckets. Initially the match is unsealed and all credits are available.

A university course-registration system must debit a student's tuition hold exactly once when a seat is committed, using two-phase commit. The coordinator prepares, then performs the single irreversible debit (sealing the transaction and counting one debit). A participant can be slow but not failed; slowness only delays the prepare, never permitting a second debit. Meanwhile a pool of seat-reservation credits shifts between a reserved bucket and a free bucket as holds are placed and lifted, always conserved. Initially the transaction is unsealed and all reservation credits are free.

nl:
A subway signalling block system lets only the participant holding the current signalling epoch commit a block reservation, using two-phase commit. Each committed reservation increments both the block counter and the authorized-commit counter. A participant can be slow but not failed; a slow participant carrying an old epoch has its prepare rejected, so no stale participant ever commits. Thus every committed block is an authorized (current-epoch) commit, and the two counters stay equal. At the batch ceiling both counters recycle. Initially both are zero.
SAFETY PROPERTY: every committed block reservation is an authorized current-epoch commit (block count equals authorized-commit count).
